What is, was, or will be the case, asserted as fact.
What is wanted, doubted, denied, or not yet real. Nearly always in a clause hanging off something in the main one.
Carries a person but no tense of its own.
Built off the %1$s (%2$s), so it inherits whatever that form does.
Built off the infinitive, so it stays regular where its neighbours don\'t.
Endings attach to the whole infinitive, not the stem — which is why an irregular stem here is its own kind of deviation.
What is happening now, what happens habitually, and what is generally true. In speech it also carries the near future.
A finished action, seen whole — beginning, middle and end together. This is the tense that moves a story forward.
The background: what used to happen, what was going on, what things were like. It sets the scene the preterite acts in.
What will happen — and, just as often, conjecture about the present: wondering aloud what is probably the case.
What would happen if something else were true, and the polite register for asking. Shares its stem with the future.
Wanting, doubting, denying, hoping — anything put forward as not (yet) fact. The main clause triggers it; you don\'t choose it freely.
The subjunctive shifted into the past, and the \"if\" half of a hypothetical.
A condition still ahead: \"when\" and \"if\" clauses about what hasn\'t happened yet. Everyday Portuguese; all but extinct in Spanish.
An infinitive that takes a subject ending, so a clause can name who is doing something without going subjunctive.
